opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most common misconceptions I run into. People often treat the aligned model as if it *is* the safety solution, as if you can take a model that's gone through RLHF or some form of safety tuning, plug it into your product, and you're done. In practice, the aligned model is one component, an important one, but just one layer in a much larger system.

Think about what alignment actually gives you. It gives you a model that, on average, across a fairly general distribution of inputs, tends to refuse clearly harmful requests and tends to behave according to some broad set of policies the model developer decided on. But those policies are generic by necessity. The developer doesn't know whether you're building a customer service bot for a bank, a tutoring tool for kids, or an internal coding assistant. What counts as "safe" or "appropriate" is very different across those settings. A response about medication dosages might be perfectly fine in a clinical decision-support tool and completely inappropriate in a children's homework helper.

So the way I frame it is: the aligned model gives you a reasonable baseline, a starting prior. Then the application developer has to define what safety means *for their specific use case*: what the risks are, who the users are, what failure modes actually matter. And then you build around the model. That includes things like input and output filtering, classifiers tuned to your policies, retrieval constraints, system-level guardrails, monitoring, human review where the stakes are high, and red-teaming that's targeted at your deployment rather than generic benchmarks.

There's also a robustness point. Alignment training is known to be somewhat brittle. Jailbreaks exist, adversarial prompts exist, and fine-tuning can erode safety behaviors pretty quickly. If your entire safety story rests on the model's internal alignment holding up, you have a single point of failure. Defense in depth is the much more defensible engineering posture.

And finally, evaluation. A lot of the safety evaluations reported for models measure behavior on general-purpose benchmarks. Those numbers don't necessarily tell you how the system will behave in your product with your users. So part of taking safety seriously at the application level is building evaluations that reflect your actual risk landscape, and continuing to measure after deployment, because user behavior shifts and new attack patterns emerge.

So in short: the aligned model is necessary but not sufficient. It's the foundation, but the responsibility for safety really sits at the level of the whole system and the specific context it's deployed in.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing I'd say is that an aligned model is necessary but really not sufficient. A lot of the conversation over the last couple of years has treated alignment at the model level as if it were the whole story, where if you do your RLHF well, if you do your safety fine-tuning well, then the model behaves and the application built on top of it is therefore safe. And I just don't think that holds up once you look at how these things actually get deployed.

The way I think about it is that the model is one component in a much larger system. You have the model, but you also have the retrieval layer, you have the prompts the developer wrote, you have the tools the model can call, you have the users, who are often not the people the model was aligned for, and you have the domain the application lives in. Safety is a property of that whole system, not of the model in isolation. A model that's very good at refusing to produce harmful content in a general chat setting can still be unsafe in, say, a financial application if it hallucinates a number, or in a healthcare setting if it's confidently wrong about a dosage. Those aren't the kinds of harms that general-purpose alignment is typically optimized against.

So what the aligned model gives you is a good prior. It gives you a baseline of behavior that's reasonable across a broad distribution of inputs, and that's genuinely valuable, because it means the application developer isn't starting from zero. But the moment you move into a specific domain, the definition of what's harmful changes. The taxonomy of risks changes. And the alignment that happened at the model provider doesn't know anything about your particular context. It doesn't know what your compliance obligations are, it doesn't know which claims your users will act on, it doesn't know which failure modes are expensive for you versus merely annoying.

That's why I spend a lot of my time thinking about what sits around the model. Guardrails, evaluation, monitoring, understanding the specific failure modes of your domain, and building classifiers or checks that target those. And importantly, measuring whether any of that actually works, because a lot of safety work ends up being vibes-based. Somebody writes a system prompt that says "be careful," and that's treated as a mitigation.

So, long answer, but the short version is: the aligned model is the foundation, and you should absolutely want one, but if you're building an application and your safety story ends at "we use an aligned model," you don't really have a safety story yet.

astra-6.text:
I think an aligned language model is one component of a safe application, but it’s not sufficient on its own. You have to look at the whole system: what the model is being used for, who is interacting with it, and what happens when it makes a mistake.

For example, if a model generates a suggestion that a person reviews, that’s a very different situation from a model that can directly take an action. Even if you use the same model in both cases, the risks and the safeguards you need are different.

So I wouldn’t think of alignment as a property that lets you say, “Okay, this model is safe, now we can build anything around it.” You still need application-specific evaluation, appropriate limits on what the system can do, and ways to identify and recover from failures. And you need to ask: aligned with whose expectations, and in what context? Those questions don’t disappear just because the model has been trained to follow instructions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think an aligned language model is one component of a safe application, but it doesn’t give you safety on its own. You have to think about the entire system: what the model is being asked to do, what information it has access to, what actions it can take, and who is affected when it makes a mistake.

For example, a model that produces a bad recommendation has very different consequences depending on whether a person reviews it or the application automatically acts on it. The underlying model might be exactly the same, but the risk is very different.

So I would start with the application and ask what failures we’re trying to prevent. Then we can work out which of those we can address through model alignment, which need constraints or checks elsewhere in the system, and where we need human oversight. And we have to evaluate that whole setup in the context where people will actually use it.
